open_questions.content: [Faculty of Computing] Cafeteria kitchen grease-laden exhaust: every faculty brief includes a cafeteria/canteen, so this applies beyond my site. Kitchen exhaust ducts carrying grease vapour are a recognised fire hazard — grease accumulates on duct walls and can ignite from a cookline flare-up, and fire can travel inside the duct through otherwise fire-separated compartments. Practical implications for any faculty planning a cafeteria: (1) use a dedicated, continuously welded or flanged liquid-tight grease duct (not ordinary galvanised spiral duct) with access doors at each change of direction for cleaning; (2) enclose the duct in a fire-rated shaft or apply a listed fire-rated wrap where it passes through or adjacent to other occupancies, and terminate it well clear of air intakes, windows and combustible roof build-up; (3) provide a dedicated kitchen suppression system (hood + duct) interlocked to shut down the supply fan and fuel, plus a grease trap/interceptor on the drainage line; (4) keep the kitchen separated from dining and teaching spaces by a fire-rated wall with self-closing doors. Worth deciding early because it drives ceiling void depth, roof penetrations and shaft locations in the zoning layout.

[Faculty of Business] Cafeteria/kitchen finding relevant to every faculty (all share the same brief): standard lightweight drywall/gypsum-board partitions and suspended mineral-fibre ceilings are unsuitable in commercial kitchen and dishwash zones — grease-laden vapour and sustained moisture destroy them and they are not washable. Kitchens need non-combustible, non-porous, washable surfaces (stainless or FRP wall panels, cement/glass-mat board rather than paper-faced gypsum), a grease duct enclosed to the same fire rating as the compartment, and wet-chemical hood suppression. Also: the kitchen is a high fire-hazard compartment (typically 60-min separation from lecture/office areas), and dining/kitchen floors need coved, slip-resistant, tanked wet-area finishes with falls to drains — not the same floor build-up as dry teaching spaces. Worth deciding early, since it changes the structural grid, drainage, and compartmentation of any cafeteria block.

[Faculty of Arts] Geotechnical caution for any faculty on stratified (layered) soil: "suitable for standard shallow spread footings" is a statement about bearing capacity, not about uniformity. On a layered profile, bearing capacity and stiffness change with the depth and thickness of each stratum, so a single large footprint (e.g. a column-free lecture hall or a long spine block) can straddle a stratum transition and settle differentially even though every individual footing passes. Practical implications that apply regardless of building type: (1) verify stratum continuity with a borehole/test-pit grid across the whole footprint, not one central hole; (2) keep column bases on the same stratum where possible, or step/ deepen footings across the transition; (3) where a large-span or heavily loaded area cannot avoid the transition, consider a stiffened strip or raft to redistribute settlement; (4) design drainage and ground-floor slabs to tolerate small differential movement (movement joints, flexible services connections). Worth a line in your survey even if your site is flat and level.

[Faculty of Engineering] Cafeteria/kitchen wet-zone material warning (relevant to every faculty, since all six briefs include a cafeteria/canteen): gypsum plasterboard partitions/ceilings and standard timber-based linings are unsuitable for commercial kitchen and wash-down zones. They degrade under repeated wet cleaning and grease-laden airborne moisture, harbour mould in the paper facing, and cannot deliver the hygiene, moisture and fire performance a kitchen requires. Specify cementitious board, masonry or tiled concrete for kitchen walls, resin/epoxy or safety-vinyl floor screeds with coved skirting and trapped channel drainage, and washable metal/vinyl-faced ceilings — no gypsum board in wet or grease zones. Also note: a kitchen's high fire load and grease ducting need a fire-rated (typically 60–120 min) non-combustible enclosure separating it from the dining area, which is easier to achieve in masonry/concrete than in lightweight drywall.
